newsitem.title: USA: House passes U.S. balanced budget legislation.
newsitem.headline: House passes U.S. balanced budget legislation.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives passed a balanced budget bill on Wednesday that jubilant supporters claimed would break Washington's long habit of deficit spending and give an extra boost to an already booming economy.

Just a day after President Bill Clinton and congressional leaders with much pomp formally announced a five-year budget agreement, House Republican leaders pushed the measure to the floor where it passed by an overwhelming 346-85 margin.
Passage was especially sweet for Republican leaders, who made deficit reduction and tax cuts a top priority.

"(This) represents the dawning of a new era. It's an era where we recognise the limits of government and begin one more time to count on ... the innovation, the creativity and the pure energy of the American people," said House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, an Ohio Republican.
Thirty-two Republicans voted against the bill joined by 53 Democrats, including House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt.

Democratic opponents complained voters had been sold a flawed package. They praised a $24 billion children's health initiative, but charged Medicare and Medicaid faced deep cuts to pay for tax cuts that would mainly benefit the rich.
"We've got a lousy bill. We'd have been better if we stayed home," said California Democratic Representative Pete Stark.
Pointing out that the budget is already moving toward balance, some economists worry the tax cuts will increase the deficit but do little to help an already charged-up economy.
The Senate also began debating the spending measure on Wednesday, as leaders rushed to clear it by week's end along with a companion bill cutting taxes by a net $94 billion.
White House officials and top lawmakers huddled until the early hours to flesh out details of the budget bill and did not agree to a final tax measure on Wednesday afternoon.

Despite grandiose rhetoric, the measure approved by the House would not by itself balance the budget by 2002. It cuts spending by about $130 billion over five years, with the bulk of reductions coming from Medicare.
It further directs Congress to find roughly $140 billion more in spending trims over that time period, but does not specify where the reductions should come from.
Critics charged future Congresses would never muster the political will to cut veterans, education, nutrition and other sensitive programmes, making the bill an empty promise.

"This is an Alice in Wonderland budget process. We're going to get to the balanced budget first by increasing the deficit with retroactive tax cuts," said Oregon Democrat Peter DeFazio. "Maybe later ... (spending) cuts will go into place."
Supporters called the measure an important step, but only a first step, toward curbing the growth of government.

"You have to give President Clinton some credit, he's rejected the left wing of his party," said House Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas. "This budget is not the end of the line, it's simply another landmark on the road to fiscal responsibilty. Next year is another budget and more tax cuts."
The legislation reduces Medicare by about $115 billion over five years, largely by cutting payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers.

Beneficiaries would see monthly premiums rise from $43.80 this year to $67 in 2002. They would have an expanded menu of preventive benefits and more insurance choices -- including tax-free medical savings accounts opposed by the White House.

Lawmakers delivered a new $24 billion programme of grants for states to expand health care to the nation's 10 million uninsured children. The programme would be funded partly through a 15 cents-per-pack cigarette tax rise.
The Congressional Budget Office estimates the plan will provide coverage to about two million previously uncovered children.
The White House won welfare spending, restoring aid to hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants, creating a $3 billion welfare-to-work programme and easing Food Stamp cuts.
Medicaid insurance for the poor, elderly and disabled would fall by more than $13 billion. Most of the savings come from trimming aid to hospitals serving indigent patients.
The measure includes reductions in nutrition and education programmes and calls on regulators to auction off part of the public broadcast spectrum, raising $21 billion.

The White House won spending initiatives, while Republicans got major tax cuts. Kasich played down Clinton victories, saying Republicans "allowed the president to shape part of the paackage. We allowed him to decorate a couple of the rooms."
